faqs.a: When two similar earners marry, their combined income can push more dollars into higher tax brackets than if they stayed single - so the couple pays more. It mostly affects dual high-income couples.
When one spouse earns most of the income, joint filing lets the couple use the lower earner's unused low brackets - cutting the total bill. Single-earner families often save thousands.

Jointly wins for most couples because of the doubled standard deduction and wider brackets. Separately can win in specific cases (like income-based student loan payments or large medical deductions) - run both scenarios with a tax pro.

marriage-tax-calculator.quickAnswer: Marriage can cut your tax bill (bonus) or raise it (penalty) depending on how incomes split. For example, spouses earning $120,000 and $20,000 pay about $14,482 filing jointly vs $18,879 as two singles - a $4,397 marriage bonus. Enter both incomes to see yours.

marriage-tax-calculator.workedExample:
Spouse A $120,000, spouse B $20,000:
1. Joint: taxable = 140,000 - 29,200 = $110,800. Tax = 2,320 + 8,532 + 3,630 = $14,482.
2. Singles: A taxable $105,400 -> tax $18,338.50; B taxable $5,400 -> tax $540. Total = $18,878.50.
3. Difference = 18,878.50 - 14,482 = $4,396.50 marriage bonus.
Joint filing wins because the lower earner's unused low brackets absorb the higher earner's income.
